questions.q: What is the practical difference between adding an account to db_datareader and granting it SELECT on three named tables?
options: db_datareader reads every table in the database forever, including future tables; the granular grants read only the three named tables, unless explicitly expanded
There is no practical difference — both are exactly equivalent
db_datareader is always more secure than granular grants
Granular grants automatically apply to every future table too
questions.explain: The fixed role's scope automatically expands to new tables created later, while explicit object-level grants stay limited to exactly what was named.

questions.q: According to this lesson, when is using a built-in role like db_datareader genuinely the right choice?
options: When the account truly needs broad access, the database is small and stable, or the need is low-risk and short-lived where speed matters more than precision
In every situation, without exception
Only when the database has no sensitive data of any kind
Only for read-only reporting accounts, never for any other purpose
questions.explain: Built-in roles are the right tool when broad access genuinely matches the actual need, or when setup speed outweighs the value of precision for a low-risk, short-lived case.

questions.q: Why would object-level permissions be preferred over a built-in role for a reporting application that only needs three specific tables?
options: So the app never automatically gains access to a new, potentially sensitive table added to the database later
Because built-in roles cannot grant SELECT permission at all
Because object-level permissions run faster at query time
Because reporting apps are not allowed to use built-in roles
questions.explain: Granting only the three tables the app actually needs keeps its access from silently expanding when new tables are added — the core idea behind least privilege.

questions.q: Which object-level permission would you grant to allow an account to run a stored procedure, without granting direct table access?
options: EXECUTE
SELECT
ALTER
INSERT
questions.explain: EXECUTE grants permission to run a stored procedure or function; the procedure can then perform its own operations without the caller needing direct table permissions.

questions.q: What system view does this lesson point to for auditing what permissions an account actually has been granted?
options: sys.database_permissions
sys.dm_exec_requests
sys.partitions
sys.dm_os_wait_stats
questions.explain: sys.database_permissions lets a DBA audit what's actually been granted, which supports revisiting and tightening access decisions over time rather than treating them as permanent.
